settings.heading: Manifesto
settings.intro: If you care about where the world is headed and you're tired of watching broken systems run on autopilot, you're already in the fight. This is what we believe—and why we're building a movement big enough to rewrite the rules.

settings.heading: Good intentions, different timelines
settings.text:
Whether an idea comes from the left or the right, it usually starts in the same place: a belief that people deserve meaningful, secure, flourishing lives. Most people aren't trying to make the world worse. They disagree on how to fix it—and when the fix should arrive.

One instinct looks to the long term. It wants to build the infrastructure, technology, and wealth that make a better tomorrow possible, even if it asks for patience today. Another instinct looks at the present. It asks who is hurting right now, and refuses to accept futures built on endless sacrifice.

Both instincts are right about something vital. A society that only manages today never builds the capacity to change. A society that sacrifices today for a distant promise forgets the people it claims to serve.

settings.heading: Progress on a human timeline
settings.text:
The future is not a moral blank cheque. We can only ask people to trade away so much of their time, health, security, and dignity for a payoff that might arrive decades from now. Progress that abandons the living isn't progress.

We don't have to treat today and tomorrow as enemies. We back projects that do both:

  • reduce suffering now while building long-term capacity
  • put useful infrastructure in people's hands today
  • protect the future without making the present unbearable
  • measure success by human flourishing, not only growth charts

A decent system never forces us to choose between immediate care and long-term hope.
Build the future without abandoning the present.

settings.heading: Solutions hiding in plain sight
settings.text:
Here's the irritating part—and the hopeful part: many of the biggest problems we face already have real, workable answers. Nobody talks about them, or broken incentives keep them sidelined. Money nobody can switch off or quietly debase. Community living that breaks isolation. Human-scale work that doesn't burn people out. Open tools owned by everyone. Global solidarity that crosses borders instead of drawing walls.

Systems rarely fix themselves out of generosity. Institutions protect their own power until the pressure gets too loud to ignore. So our strategy starts with visibility: put the obvious, high-potential solutions in front of everyone. When people know what to push for and vote for, politicians have a much harder time pretending there's no alternative.

And when entrenched systems still refuse to budge? History is clear: organized, peaceful collective refusal works. We don't have all the answers, and we aren't waiting for permission to figure them out together.

settings.heading: Turn the tools around
settings.text:
Right now, platforms, algorithms, and AI are mostly pointed in one direction: shaping what we buy, what we click, and what we think. Concentrated power loves a one-way street. We believe those exact same tools belong in people's hands.

AI changes the equation fast, and we won't pretend it's harmless. The obvious danger is that it churns out more closed tools for already dominant companies, making a top-heavy system even harder to challenge. The real question isn't whether a machine helped write the code. It's who can inspect it, use it, improve it, and own what gets built around it.

AI-assisted work only becomes a public good when humans take responsibility—reviewing it, testing it, documenting it, and releasing it under a clear licence. Our principle is simple. Use the machines to build tools that make people less dependent on the machines' owners.
Use their tools for our benefit.

settings.heading: Build the commons
settings.text:
Open source isn't a technical hobby. It's shared public infrastructure—a quiet rebellion against the idea that every useful tool must be owned, rented, and fenced in by a giant platform.

A closed tool turns us into users. An open tool turns us into participants. Most corporate platforms aren't powered by magic; the hard parts are trust, maintenance, and governance. Building in the open redirects value where it belongs:

  • from rented access to shared infrastructure
  • from passive consumption to active contribution
  • from closed black boxes to inspectable tools
  • from value concentrated in a few hands to capacity built together

Software shapes how we talk, work, learn, and organize. You don't need to start a company to improve it. You can fix a bug, translate a page, write documentation, test a release, or help maintain something thousands of people rely on. Useful things should not disappear behind a login screen.

We hold ourselves to the same standard: whenever we use automation or AI, we say so plainly and publish the details in how we use AI.

settings.heading: Revolt peacefully. Build what's next.
settings.text: What you're already doing matters—let's build on it together. It's time to take matters into our own hands, learn how to stop this, and join the cause for systems that actually serve people.

settings.title: Technofeudalism
settings.author: Yanis Varoufakis
settings.note: Argues that cloud platforms have replaced markets with something closer to fiefdoms. It also remembers that the first internet ran on common, open protocols that anyone could use for free.

settings.title: The Man Who Quit Money
settings.author: Mark Sundeen
settings.note: Daniel Suelo stopped using money. The book asks how much of our relationship with money is necessary—and how much we have simply accepted by default.

settings.title: Broken Money
settings.author: Lyn Alden
settings.note: A history of money as a ledger, and of why the financial system fails so many of the people who depend on it.

settings.title: The Price of Tomorrow
settings.author: Jeff Booth
settings.note: Technology keeps making things cheaper. An economy built on ever-growing credit has to fight that.

settings.title: Sapiens
settings.author: Yuval Noah Harari
settings.note: How shared stories—money among them—let millions of strangers cooperate.

settings.title: Island
settings.author: Aldous Huxley
settings.note: Huxley’s last novel imagines a small society organised around human flourishing, and asks what it would take to protect it.

settings.name: Yanis Varoufakis
settings.note: Economist and former Greek finance minister. Author of Technofeudalism.

settings.name: Jonathan Haidt
settings.note: Social psychologist. Writes about how social media changes childhood and public life.

settings.name: Daniel Suelo
settings.note: Lived for years without money. The subject of The Man Who Quit Money.

settings.name: Judy Heumann
settings.note: Disability rights activist who fought for access as a civil right.

settings.heading: Influences
settings.intro: The books and people that formed our views. We do not agree with everything any of them says.
